content.overview: Curing can change moisture distribution and sensory or chemical attributes, but it is not a universal recipe and cannot erase an uncontrolled drying history or confirmed contamination.

vocabulary.definition: Controlled holding intended to allow defined product changes or equilibration.
Movement toward a more uniform condition within material or between product and package headspace.
Recorded sequence of conditions and handling experienced by a lot.

sections.title: Curing begins with known input
sections.body: The incoming lot should have defined identity, drying history and product condition; curing should not be used to make unknown material appear acceptable.

sections.title: Moisture can redistribute
sections.body: Sealed or semi-closed conditioning can change measured product condition, so representative monitoring and controlled handling remain necessary.

sections.title: Outcomes depend on product and process
sections.body: Time, temperature, oxygen, container and starting condition interact. Published results support variables to control, not one universal duration or endpoint.

workedExamples: A lot with an unexplained wet zone should remain under investigation rather than being blended into curing to average the condition.
commonMistakes: Treating curing as a sanitation step.
Using aroma alone as release evidence.
Starting cure without preserving drying history.
content.practicalApplication: Define an intake, monitoring and exception record for a curing lot while keeping endpoint authority explicit.
content.summary: Controlled curing preserves identity and measured condition; it does not erase upstream deviations.
